scholar.label: Jason W. Carter
scholar.description: Jason W. Carter is a scholar of ancient philosophy at the University of Glasgow (institutional affiliation given at the end of the article body, p. 52: 'University of Glasgow'). He previously worked at the University of St Andrews, where this paper was developed (the article is dedicated to Sarah Broadie, 'whilst we were colleagues at St Andrews'). His work focuses on Aristotle's logic, modal concepts, theory of truth, and psychology; this article reconstructs Aristotle's refutation of logical fatalism in De Interpretatione 9 using a Priorean tense logic.

publication.label: Carter — Fatalism and False Futures in De Interpretatione 9
publication.description: Article reconstructing Aristotle's refutation of logical fatalism in De Interpretatione 9. Carter rejects the two dominant ancient interpretations (the 'oldest', Peripatetic/Simplicius reading that PB and RCP fail to apply to future contingents until the event occurs; and the 'second oldest', Ammonius/Boethius reading that future pairs are 'indefinitely' true or false). In their place he revives a third 'both-false' interpretation (ascribed by Boethius to certain unnamed sixth-century philosophers): future contingent statements obey the Principle of Bivalence but violate the Rule of Contradictory Pairs by both being false. Using a modified Priorean tense logic he shows Aristotle accepts Future Truth Necessity but denies Retro-Truth and Eternal Truth, citing GC 2.11 and Posterior Analytics 2.12 as decisive extra-textual evidence.

metadata.year_verification_note: Published 2024 (OUP, 6 Jun 2024); 'Winter 2022' is the OSAP vol. 63 spine label, not the year. Confirmed via St Andrews Research Portal and Crossref.

arguments.label: Carter: the 'both-false' interpretation of De Int. 9
arguments.description: Carter's central thesis: Aristotle's implicit solution to the logical argument for fatalism is that future contingent singular statements follow the Principle of Bivalence (PB) but violate the Rule of Contradictory Pairs (RCP) by 'both being false'. This 'third' interpretation is revived against the 'oldest' (PB/RCP suspended for future contingents) and 'second oldest' (Ammonius/Boethius: each member true-or-false but not 'definitely') readings. Verbatim (p. 7): 'This interpretation holds that Aristotle thought that future contingent statements follow PB but violate RCP by both being false.' Carter notes Boethius reports unnamed sixth-century philosophers holding this view (p. 7, citing Boeth., In De int., 2nd edn 2.215, 15-24).

verbatim_evidence.quote: This interpretation holds that Aristotle thought that future contingent statements follow PB but violate RCP by both being false.

arguments.label: Carter: PB / LEM / RCP distinguished; refutation targets RCP
arguments.description: Carter distinguishes three semantic principles that scholars take Aristotle to reject one or more of: the Principle of Bivalence (PB: 'For every proposition p, necessarily, p is either true or false'), the Law of Excluded Middle (LEM: 'For every proposition p, necessarily, either p is true or not-p is true'), and the Rule of Contradictory Pairs (RCP: 'For every pair of contradictory Aristotelian statements, one member of the pair is true, and the other false'). RCP presupposes both PB and LEM but is not equivalent to the Law of Non-Contradiction. Carter argues, with others before him, that Aristotle's refutation of fatalism targets RCP, not PB. Crucially Aristotle 'has already established that one can assume PB without assuming RCP (see DI 9, 18a31-32)' (p. 24).

verbatim_evidence.quote: RULE OF CONTRADICTORY PAIRS (RCP) =def: For every pair of contradictory Aristotelian statements, one member of the pair is true, and the other false.

arguments.label: Carter: reconstruction of Aristotle's first fatalist argument (DI 9, 18a34-b4)
arguments.description: Carter reconstructs the first of two fatalist arguments Aristotle reports (DI 9, 18a34-b4) as valid, resting on three tense-logical principles formulated in a modified Prior tense logic: Present Necessity (Tp -> [box]p), Retro-Truth (p -> TPFp), and Retro-Necessity (TPFp -> [box]PFp). The argument shows that if RCP holds of present-tense statements that refer to now-necessary events, then via Retro-Truth/Retro-Necessity RCP carries to future-tense statements indexed to the past, and so the future event is now necessary. Carter argues this first argument is valid but Aristotle does not think it sound, because the past time it appeals to is not explicitly quantified (a bridging principle is missing, supplied by the second argument).

verbatim_evidence.quote: Present Necessity: Tp → □p ... Retro-Truth: p → TPFp ... Retro-Necessity: TPFp → □PFp

arguments.label: Carter: reconstruction of Aristotle's second fatalist argument (DI 9, 18b9-16)
arguments.description: Carter reconstructs the stronger, second fatalist argument (DI 9, 18b9-16), which introduces two further bridging principles: Eternal Truth (TPFp -> HTFp, 'if it was the case that it would be the case that p, it has always been true that it would be the case that p') and Eternal Necessity (HTFp -> H[box]Fp). Carter argues this argument is again valid but unsound. Aristotle would accept Eternal Necessity (he commits to it in De Caelo 1.12, 337b35-338a4: what always exists necessarily exists). Therefore, to escape fatalism, Aristotle must deny either Retro-Truth or Eternal Truth (or both) - which forces the question of what truth value future contingent statements have.

verbatim_evidence.quote: Eternal Truth: TPFp → HTFp ... Eternal Necessity: HTFp → H□Fp

arguments.label: Carter: the two arguments against the both-false view are themselves fatalist arguments
arguments.description: Against scholarly consensus (Gaskin, Ackrill) that Aristotle speaks in propria persona when objecting to the both-false solution (DI 9, 18b17-25), Carter argues the two objections are 'much more plausibly viewed as two additional fatalist arguments'. The first objection (18b17-20) begs the question by assuming RCP - exactly what the fatalist, not Aristotle, believes (Aristotle holds future contingents are exceptions to RCP, 18a28-34). The second objection (18b20-25, the sea-battle case) rests on Future Truth Necessity (TFp -> [box]Fp) and Future Falsity Necessity; both are illegitimate given Aristotle's two-sided theory of possibility (DI 13, 22b20-1: 'if a thing is possible to be, it is at the same time possible also not to be').

verbatim_evidence.quote: The arguments against the both-false view, as we shall see, because of their tense-logical assumptions, are much more plausibly viewed as two additional fatalist arguments.

arguments.label: Carter: Aristotle accepts Future Truth Necessity (modal semantics of 'will be', GC 2.11)
arguments.description: Carter argues that, for modally unqualified future tense statements, Aristotle accepts the fatalist's principle Future Truth Necessity (TFp -> [box]Fp): an unqualified affirmation or denial of a singular future contingent event 'by default will express that the occurrence or non-occurrence of that future contingent event is necessary'. The decisive evidence is De Generatione et Corruptione 2.11 (337b3-9), where Aristotle distinguishes 'will be' (estai, picks out an event that must - dei - be the case at some future time) from 'is going to be' (mellei, compatible with non-occurrence). A modal-possibility reading of 'will be' is rejected because it would make future contradictory pairs always both true (DI 12, 21b13-22), which cannot be Aristotle's view since he holds future contingents can form contradictory pairs (DI 9, 19a36-7).

verbatim_evidence.quote: an affirmation or denial of a singular future contingent event that does not explicitly contain the modal operator ‘possibly’ (or some similar qualification), by default will express that the occurrence or non-occurrence of that future contingent event is necessary.

arguments.label: Carter: Posterior Analytics 2.12 shows Aristotle denies Retro-Truth (extra-textual evidence)
arguments.description: Carter's strongest extra-textual argument: in Posterior Analytics 2.12 Aristotle holds that of causally related but non-simultaneous events, in the interval after cause A occurs but before effect C occurs, 'it will be false to say that already the other [event, C,] has come to be' (95a30-31), and one cannot validly deduce in the future tense that C will be from the fact that A has come to be. Because Retro-Truth (p -> TPFp) is built on precisely the illicit cause-to-effect, tense-shifting reasoning Aristotle rules out in Post. An. 2.12, Aristotle's considered view must be that Retro-Truth is invalid; since Eternal Truth depends on Retro-Truth, both fatalist principles fall. Hence Aristotle explicitly endorses that unqualified future contingent affirmations and denials are 'false during the interval between their prediction and their taking place' (Conclusion, p. 48-49).

verbatim_evidence.quote: If so, then this passage also reveals something wholly unexpected, which is that Aristotle cannot accept Retro-Truth.

arguments.label: Carter: the cost of the both-false view (contraries, not contradictories)
arguments.description: Carter acknowledges the price of the both-false reading: on it, the modally-disguised future contingent affirmation and denial of DI 9 ('There will be a sea battle tomorrow' / 'There will not be') are not genuine contradictories but contraries, since the true contradictory of 'There necessarily will be a sea battle' is 'There will not necessarily be a sea battle' (= 'There possibly will not be'). Once modally undisguised, future pairs follow RCP and LEM normally. Aristotle treats them as contradictories only because he had not yet (until DI 12-14) worked out the contrary/contradictory distinction for modal statements, and allowed syntactic form to count as sufficient for contradiction (cf. DI 7, 17b9-10; DI 8, 18a19-27). Carter judges this 'a cost worth accepting' because it lets Aristotle refute fatalism without sacrificing PB or LEM.

verbatim_evidence.quote: on the both-false view, the future contingent affirmations and denials that Aristotle considers in DI 9 turn out to be not true contradictory pairs, but contrary pairs.
